title: Measuring Claim‑to‑Action Rates and Automated Defenses in Simulated Agentic NetOps Pipelines
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (hosted-netops-gvr-v1) to measure how often LLM‑produced network configuration proposals would trigger unsafe simulated deployments (claim→action) and whether an automated defended pipeline reduces that rate relative to an unguarded baseline. We generated 300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks and ran paired baseline and guarded conditions; 272 complete pairs were analyzable. On those 272 pairs the observed contingency was n11=271, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0 (baseline safe rate = 271/272 = 0.9963235; guarded safe rate = 272/272 = 1.0). The absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00367647; paired‑bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00000, 0.01102941] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. A verified orchestration deviation occurred: the preregistered multimodel consensus ensemble stage did not execute (execution manifest documents the stage_counts). All per‑episode responses, validator traces, provider traces, scoring JSONs, and per‑file SHA‑256 hashes are archived and referenced in the Disclosure. We report the artifact‑grounded numeric results, the verified deviation, preregistered conservative sensitivity analyses, and operational implications for validator‑based defenses in agentic NetOps evaluation.

sections.introduction:
Motivation and goal. Increasingly agentic pipelines convert operator intent (natural language) into concrete NetOps actions (config edits, tool calls). When fluent LLM text becomes an action, misinterpretation or unsupported state changes can lead to misconfiguration, outages, or policy violations. Systematic, reproducible measurement of how often LLM claims would fire concrete (simulated) actions—the claim→action rate—and whether automated defenses can reduce that rate is critical for trustworthy NetOps automation.
Research question and contribution. We preregistered a paired experiment whose primary estimand is the paired difference in safe execution rates between a defended pipeline and an unguarded baseline. Our contribution is an artifact‑anchored empirical measurement (responses, per‑episode deterministic validation traces, provider traces, full SHA‑256 manifest) and a documented operational finding: deterministic validators produce auditable adjudication and can nearly eliminate unsafe simulated deployments in this synthetic setting, but a preregistered multimodel ensemble stage was not executed and therefore its effect remains untested in this run.
sections.related_work: Closest prior work spans deterministic network verification (NetKAT, header‑space, SMT‑based tools) and recent LLM‑for‑AIOps/agentic NetOps studies proposing generate–validate–repair and tool‑augmented agents. Deterministic validators and generate–validate architectures are common recommendations in both NetOps and LLM‑agent literature; our study differs by preregistering the estimand, archiving full per‑episode validator traces, and reporting verified orchestration deviations with a complete per‑file SHA‑256 manifest to enable deterministic audit.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study (hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-26) preregistered the primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in safe execution rates on paired tasks). The preregistration (SHA‑256: fe21c23a6a1987ff442f57e5a44c84ffb1266b9920cf348d6bf1c41520e6cebe) fixed design choices: paired binary design, planned N=300 tasks, complete‑pair primary analysis, McNemar exact two‑sided confirmatory test, paired‑bootstrap CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729), single automatic retry policy, and a conservative sensitivity treating failed provider calls as unsafe.
Task generation and simulator. A deterministic task generator produced synthetic intent→configuration tasks that encode operational invariants (must‑be‑down-before‑mtu, minimum‑up groups, ordered sequences). Each task includes initial state, required sequence, and canonical reference configuration. Tasks and task manifest are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 3d7b63c361c9848b20750cc44125f195f0341346d48393ce72ae07d6c0fea745).
Pipelines and scorer. Baseline: single LLM generation converted to configuration and evaluated by a deterministic network validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Guarded (preregistered): deterministic validator + 3‑model consensus + simulated human gate. Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 executes purely syntactic/semantic parsing of commands, simulator reachability/state check, and emits structured validator_trace (parsed_command_count, touched fields, final simulated state, violation codes). The scorer produced a binary safe/unsafe outcome per episode and an artifact JSON (execution/scoring/*.json) with validator_trace embedded.
Execution and archival. The run was executed under adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. All raw responses, scoring JSONs, provider traces, validator traces, execution logs, and per‑file SHA‑256s are archived; the execution manifest records model_calls_used = 301 and provider‑call audit counts (completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 273; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 28) (execution/execution_manifest.json). The archived model configuration declares the model used (gpt-5-mini; execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256 = 9b382b55...).
Missingness and sensitivity. Complete pairs are defined per preregistration (both modes yield a parsable binary outcome). Episodes with failed model calls after the allowed retry are recorded as failed. Primary analysis uses complete pairs only (N=272). Conservative preregistered sensitivity treats failed episodes as unsafe on planned N=300.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (archival evidence). Planned episodes = 600 (paired design); completed episodes = 544; failed episodes = 56. Provider‑call audit: model_calls_used = 301; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 273; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 28 (execution/execution_manifest.json; full per‑file SHA‑256 manifest archived). Primary contingency (complete pairs). Complete pairs analyzable = 272 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 = 682a629a...). Observed contingency counts (complete pairs N=272): n11 = 271, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Observed safe rates: baseline = 271/272 = 0.9963235294; guarded = 272/272 = 1.0. Absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.003676470588235281.
Inference and uncertainty (artifact‑computed). Paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) = [0.00000, 0.011029411764705883] (analysis log archived). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Conservative sensitivity. Treating the 28 failed provider calls as unsafe on planned N=300 yields baseline safe = 271/300 = 0.90333333; guarded safe = 272/300 = 0.90666667; absolute difference = 0.00333333. Representative episode artifacts. Representative scoring JSONs and responses are archived (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json SHA‑256 = 465d73fd..., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 = b227731a...); execution/responses/*.txt contain the exact generated configurations and are hashed in the manifest.
Verified orchestration deviation (artifact evidence). The preregistered guarded pipeline specified validator + 3‑model consensus + simulated human gate. The execution manifest documents stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation":300, "repair":1} and condition_counts = {"shared":300, "guarded":1}; provider‑call audit shows model_calls_used = 301 and 28 failed calls. These artifact fields prove the multimodel consensus stage did not execute in this archived run; the guarded condition as archived therefore evaluates deterministic validator + simulated human gate on a single shared generation rather than the preregistered ensemble. All such provenance fields and per‑file SHA‑256 values are archived for deterministic audit (execution/execution_manifest.json).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation. The executed guarded pipeline (deterministic validator + simulated human gate applied to a single generation) yields near‑perfect guarded acceptance on analyzable pairs, but the absolute paired improvement over baseline is tiny and statistically inconclusive given observed discordant counts (n10=1, n01=0) and p = 1.0. Because the preregistered ensemble stage did not run, this execution cannot evaluate the ensemble hypothesis; the archived run instead provides an artifact‑grounded lesson about validator gating and orchestration reliability.
Operational implications. Deterministic validators produce machine‑readable, auditable traces that enable reproducible adjudication and failure diagnosis (see execution/scoring/*.json). In synthetic topologies with encoded safety invariants, validator gating plus a human gate can prevent unsafe simulated deployments. However, robust orchestration (retries, caching, monitoring) is required to test ensemble defenses and to preserve planned power; provider failures materially reduced the effective sample here.
Threats to validity. Internal validity: single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and a single run; prompt sensitivity and non‑determinism remain concerns despite cached responses and per‑call seeds. Construct validity: synthetic task bank and deterministic simulator simplify real vendor/state behavior; validator invariants define what counts as unsafe. External validity: results do not generalize to production hardware or richer topologies without further evaluation. Conclusion validity: provider failures reduced effective N and lowered power to detect small absolute effects; the preregistered ensemble was not tested due to an execution deviation.
Peer‑review required item and archival resolution. Reviewers requested realized prompt‑family counts (benign/ambiguous/adversarial) for (a) the planned N=300 tasks, (b) the analyzable complete pairs N=272, and (c) the 28 failed episodes. Those counts are deterministically derivable from the archived task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 3d7b63c361c9848b20750cc44125f195f0341346d48393ce72ae07d6c0fea745). The supplied analysis outputs accompanying this manuscript do not include a precomputed per‑family summary file; therefore we do not report per‑family numeric counts in the text rather than invent values. The canonical manifest path and SHA‑256 above enable deterministic reconstruction of the exact requested counts from the archived artifact; a follow‑up extraction from execution/task_manifest.jsonl will produce the exact per‑family counts without new model calls. This manuscript explicitly documents that path and SHA‑256 so that reviewers and auditors can reproduce the counts from the authoritative archive.
Recommended re‑execution to complete preregistration. To evaluate the preregistered ensemble hypothesis, re‑run the protocol under hardened orchestration (deterministic caching, robust retries, run‑time monitors) so that stage_counts in execution manifest match the preregistered design; this will also mitigate failed call loss of power.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed an artifact‑anchored paired evaluation of claim→action risk in agentic NetOps pipelines. The archived run produced 272 analyzable paired outcomes with near‑perfect guarded acceptance under the executed pipeline (validator + simulated human gate on a single generation). A verified orchestration deviation prevented execution of the preregistered multimodel ensemble stage; hence the ensemble effect remains untested in this run. All raw responses, per‑episode scoring JSONs, provider traces, validator traces, and a full per‑file SHA‑256 manifest are archived to permit deterministic verification. The principal evidence‑grounded conclusion: deterministic validators provide auditable adjudication and, in this simulated setting, can substantially reduce unsafe simulated executions, but ensemble defenses require a follow‑up run under robust orchestration to be empirically assessed. The archive and SHA‑256 manifest support reproducible re‑execution and independent verification.

limitations: Single declared model present in the archived execution (declared model = "gpt-5-mini"); no multi‑model generality claims are supported by this run.
Synthetic tasks and a deterministic simulator were used; construct and external validity versus vendor hardware and production topologies are limited.

A verified execution deviation occurred: the preregistered multimodel consensus ensemble stage did not run; the archived guarded condition therefore evaluates a different pipeline (validator + simulated human gate on a single shared generation).
Provider call failures (28 failed hosted model calls) reduced the effective sample and limited power to detect small absolute effects.
